synopsis: Paddock co-authored RAND’s Driving to Safety with Kalra; the corpus dates it to April 2016, with Chapter 7 specifying 12 April 2016 [f5464, f6920]. Its analysis required 275 million failure-free miles to show, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement with 80% power [f6662, f6663]. The glossary summarizes the broader requirements as hundreds of millions and sometimes hundreds of billions of road miles, taking existing fleets tens and sometimes hundreds of years [f15812, f14264]. Chapter 12 uses these on-road findings as the statistical rationale for virtual testing, concluding that driving tests alone cannot demonstrate safety at low failure rates; the supplied facts do not establish equivalent mileage requirements for heavy off-road machines [f9755, f6662, f6663].

relations.note: Both date the same RAND report to April 2016; Chapter 7 specifies the day.
Provides a specific hundreds-of-millions mileage requirement and its confidence threshold.
Specifies mileage, improvement target, and statistical power for one safety comparison.
The large failure-free mileage requirement supports the rationale for virtual testing.
Billions of miles for demonstrating improvement support the limitations of driving tests alone.
Decades-to-centuries testing times support pursuing virtual testing.
Enormous road-mile requirements explain why driving tests alone are insufficient.
Expresses required road distances as testing times for existing fleets.
